title: GCD Sort of an Array
statement:
You may rearrange the integer array `nums` with a single kind of move, repeated as often as you like: choose two positions `i` and `j` whose values have a common divisor larger than 1 (that is, `gcd(nums[i], nums[j]) > 1`) and exchange the two values.

Return `true` if some sequence of such moves (possibly none) leaves `nums` in non-decreasing order, and `false` if no sequence does.
notes:
## Intuition

Treat each value as a token. Two tokens that share a prime factor may trade places, and by chaining trades through intermediate tokens, any tokens that are linked by a path of shared primes can be arranged in any order over the positions they occupy. Example 1 shows this: `7` and `3` never swap directly, but both share a prime with `21`.

Building that graph by testing every pair with `gcd` costs O(n²), too slow for 3·10⁴ values. Instead, link every number to each of its prime factors in a union-find: two numbers end up in the same set exactly when a chain of shared primes connects them. The array is sortable when, at every position, the current value and the value that belongs there after sorting lie in the same set.

## Approach

1. Let `maxValue` be the largest number and make a union-find `parent` over `0..maxValue`; its nodes stand for both values and primes.
2. Sieve `smallestPrime[v]` for every `v` up to `maxValue`.
3. For each `num`, peel off its distinct primes with `smallestPrime` and join each `prime` with `num`.
4. Sort a copy into `sorted`. If `find(nums[i])` differs from `find(sorted[i])` for some `i`, return `false`.
5. Otherwise return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [7, 21, 3]`, `maxValue = 21`. For `7`, the only prime is `7`, the same node. For `21`, prime `3` joins `21`, then prime `7` joins `21`. For `3`, prime `3` is already with `21`. Now `3`, `7` and `21` share one root. `sorted = [3, 7, 21]`: the pairs `(7, 3)`, `(21, 7)` and `(3, 21)` all have equal roots, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(M log log M + n log M + n log n) with `M = maxValue`: the sieve, factoring each number into at most log M primes, and the sort.
- Space: O(M) for `parent` and `smallestPrime`.

## Pitfalls

- Requiring each misplaced value to swap directly with the value it must trade with is too strict; chains through other numbers count.
- The union-find is keyed by values and primes, so it needs `maxValue + 1` slots, not `n`.
- Testing all pairs with `gcd` is correct but quadratic and times out at the full limits.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `maxValue` | the largest number in `nums` |
| `parent`, `find` | union-find over values and primes |
| `smallestPrime` | smallest prime factor of each value up to `maxValue` |
| `p`, `multiple` | sieve counter and the multiples it marks |
| `num`, `rest`, `prime` | the number being factored, what is left of it, and its current prime |
| `sorted` | a sorted copy of `nums` |
| `i` | the position being compared |

narration.2: The largest value decides how many union-find nodes and sieve slots are needed.
narration.3: Every value and every prime starts as its own set.
narration.5: Climb parent links until reaching a node that is its own parent, the set's root.
narration.6: Point this node at its grandparent to keep future climbs short.
narration.9: The root names the set that x belongs to.
narration.11: smallestPrime[v] will hold the smallest prime that divides v.
narration.12: Try every candidate p from 2 up to the largest value.
narration.13: A slot that is already filled has a smaller prime factor, so p is not prime.
narration.16: p is prime: visit each of its multiples.
narration.18: The first prime to reach a multiple is its smallest prime factor.
narration.22: Now link each number with its prime factors.
narration.24: Keep peeling primes off until nothing is left of the number.
narration.25: The smallest remaining prime factor comes straight from the sieve.
narration.26: Join the prime's set with the number's set; numbers sharing this prime meet here.
narration.27: Divide out every copy of this prime so the next one found is different.
narration.32: Sort a copy to see which value must end up at each position.
narration.34: The value here and the value that belongs here must be in the same set to be exchanged.
narration.35: Different sets: no chain of swaps can bring the right value here.
narration.38: Every position can receive its value, so the array can be sorted.
